sources.title: Tirunesh Dibaba (Q6003), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-02): label 'Tirunesh Dibaba', description 'Ethiopian long distance track athlete', born 1985-06-01, no death date (living), citizenship Ethiopia, Korean label present. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Tirunesh Dibaba' (print view, revised 28 May 2026), read in full: Ethiopian distance runner who at the 2008 Beijing Olympics became the first woman to win gold in both the 5,000 m and 10,000 m, and who won the 10,000 m again in London in 2012, the first woman to win the event at two consecutive Olympics; Olympic medals 2004 (bronze 5,000 m), 2008 (two golds), 2012 (gold 10,000 m, bronze 5,000 m), 2016 (bronze 10,000 m); 2003 world junior cross-country title, junior 5,000 m world record and the world 5,000 m title (youngest-ever world champion in her sport); the 2005 world distance double; world cross-country titles; 2013 world 10,000 m title; half-marathon debut in 2012, first marathon in 2014 and first marathon win in Chicago in 2017. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE. Concise; the passages on marriage and injuries were not used.

Joerg Wenig (IAAF), 'Dibaba is back writing Olympic history again', World Athletics news (4 August 2012), read in full: report on her 10,000 m win at London 2012 (30:20.75, a sprint over the last 500 m), with her own account that the Ethiopian team agreed a tactic with its coaches before the race, that she had planned to go at 600 or 500 m and waited until 500 m, and that she was nominated only as a reserve for the 5,000 m. The federation's own writer, so favourable; the race facts are checkable and the quoted plan is her own account. Passages on her injuries and marriage were not used.

LetsRun.com, '2012 Olympic Women's 10,000: Tirunesh Dibaba Makes The Case For Being The Greatest Ever' (3 August 2012), read in full: an independent athletics site's lap-by-lap race analysis showing Dibaba waiting in fourth for most of the last eight laps, moving up with about three laps left and taking the lead about 530 m from the finish to win by the second-largest margin in Olympic 10,000 m history; says she was nine for nine in 10,000 m races and held the 5,000 m world record (14:11.15); quotes her and the rivals Kipyego and Cheruiyot, including Kipyego's attempt to take the kick away from her; reports she announced her plan to run a marathon. Enthusiastic commentary ('greatest ever'), so the superlatives are the writers' opinion; the splits and results are factual.

Cathal Dennehy (IAAF), 'Dibaba dominates and Rupp times it right to win in Chicago', World Athletics report (8 October 2017), read in full: race report of her first marathon win (2:18:31, her third career marathon, almost two minutes clear of Brigid Kosgei), saying she led from the start without pacemakers, towed a group through 10 km in 32:28 and halfway in 1:08:48, zig-zagged to stop rivals drafting, and pulled away after 30 km; quotes her that she ran without pacemakers, that she 'worked very hard', that she skipped an award ceremony after the London world championships to prepare, and that the marathon would be her sole focus. A federation report by a staff journalist; favourable but tactically specific. A fuller account of the personal best of 2:17:56 is only mentioned in passing.

Sean Ingle, 'Dibaba confident of meeting London Marathon demands' (The Guardian, 11 April 2014, as republished by Gulf Times), read in full: pre-race profile at her marathon debut saying she had trained intensively for five months, had asked Haile Gebrselassie to share his marathon experience, had withdrawn from the 2013 London race, and that the bookmakers were sceptical of her chances; includes her own remarks that the change of event was difficult but she had done her best. Independent national newspaper; short preview, and the training claim is her own.

Laureus World Sports Awards, 2006 Sportswoman of the Year nominee profile of Tirunesh Dibaba, read in full: credits her 2005 world cross-country short and long titles and the world 5,000/10,000 m double in Helsinki, notes a closing 400 m of 58.33 s in the 10,000 m, and quotes her saying that she stuck with her usual programme without increasing distance and did not allow anything outside running to interrupt her training. An award body's promotional profile quoting her own words; self-report, favourable.

Athletics Illustrated, 'Tirunesh Dibaba where is the recognition?' (2013), read in full: an opinion note after her 2013 world 10,000 m win summarising her record (a perfect 11 for 11 in 10,000 m races, five world cross-country golds, three world 10,000 m titles and two Olympic ones) and listing her personal bests and her Olympic, world and world cross-country medals; relays a LetsRun article. Short, partly derivative opinion, used only to corroborate the results list.

persistence.rationale: [src_dibaba_britannica, src_dibaba_ai, src_dibaba_wa2017, src_dibaba_guardian, src_dibaba_laureus | 2001-2017 | reference biography + athletics magazine + federation report + national newspaper + award body] Britannica's list of medals and titles runs from her 2001 junior debut and 2003 world title through Olympic medals in 2004, 2008, 2012 and 2016, the 2013 world 10,000 m title and a 2017 marathon win; the Guardian says she trained intensively for five months for the 2014 marathon debut after postponing it a year; the Chicago report quotes her that she worked very hard and skipped an award ceremony to prepare; the Laureus profile quotes her on sticking to her programme. The span of top-level results across more than fifteen years and a change of event is independently documented, but the effort statements are her own and no source describes her training in detail. Time lost to injury is deliberately not used as personality evidence.

competitiveness.rationale: [src_dibaba_letsrun, src_dibaba_wa2012, src_dibaba_wa2017, src_dibaba_ai, src_dibaba_britannica | 2005-2017 | athletics site + federation reports + magazine + reference biography] LetsRun and Athletics Illustrated record a perfect run in 10,000 m finals (nine for nine in 2012, eleven for eleven by 2013), two Olympic and three world titles at that distance, and the world 5,000 m record; LetsRun's lap-by-lap account and rival Kipyego's remark show her rivals trying to take away her kick and failing; at Chicago she took the lead from the gun and zig-zagged to stop rivals drafting. A strong drive to win and a record to match are documented across independent reports, but the sources describe results and race tactics, not her motives, and LetsRun's 'greatest ever' is opinion.

planning_orientation.rationale: [src_dibaba_wa2012, src_dibaba_letsrun, src_dibaba_wa2017, src_dibaba_guardian | 2012-2017 | federation reports + athletics site + national newspaper] The federation report and LetsRun both give her account that the team agreed a plan with its coaches before the London 10,000 m, that she planned to move at 600 or 500 m and waited until 500 m, and LetsRun's splits show her sitting fourth and moving at about 530 m; the Guardian says she prepared for five months for the marathon debut and sought Gebrselassie's advice; at Chicago she led without pacemakers. A pre-race plan carried out in the race is documented, but the plan itself is her own statement and the race reports do not show how she prepared.

adaptability.rationale: [src_dibaba_britannica, src_dibaba_guardian, src_dibaba_wa2017 | 2012-2017 | reference biography + national newspaper + federation report] Britannica traces her move from track and cross-country to the half marathon in 2012, the marathon in 2014 and a win in Chicago in 2017, and the Chicago report quotes her that the marathon would be her sole focus; the Guardian quotes her saying the change of event was difficult but she had done her best. Moving between very different event types and succeeding is documented, but the three sources describe the change and not how she handled it, hence moderate confidence.

discipline.rationale: [src_dibaba_laureus, src_dibaba_wa2017, src_dibaba_guardian | 2005-2017 | award body + federation report + national newspaper] She is quoted saying in 2005 that she stuck to her usual programme without being interrupted by anything outside running, and in 2017 that she skipped an award ceremony to prepare for Chicago, while the Guardian cites five months of intensive marathon preparation. All of it is her own account relayed by a promotional profile, a federation writer and a preview; no independent observer describes her routine. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.48 because every datum is self-report.

The live Flickr page was opened and its embedded photo data shows licence value 5 (the page links https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0 and says 'Some rights reserved'; the 'All Rights Reserved' string on the page is only Flickr's list of licence names), the owner is Ragnar Singsaas (the photographer, not an agency account), and the caption identifies 'Tirunesh Dibaba of Etiopia sets new world record time 14:11:15'. Identification is positive: the race bib in the photograph reads 'DIBABA OSLO 2008' and her 5,000 m world record of 14:11.15 was set at the Oslo meeting (the Diamond League profile lists it on 6 June 2008; Flickr's timestamp reads 7 June 21:13, so the date is stated as 2008 with that caveat). This is a sports photograph, cropped by this project to head and chest (2026 x 1893 px region of the original, downscaled to 1200 x 1121, never enlarged); the sponsor's name appears on the bib. Kind likeness (a documented photograph of her). The lead's alternatives (other CC Commons images of Ethiopian athletes) were not needed. Also read but not used: the World Athletics 2009 Boston news item (nickname and records), the RunBlogRun 2014 video post and the Diamond League profile (honours list; used only to date the 5,000 m world record). Non-self behavioural sources: LetsRun's race analysis (with rivals' comments) and the two federation race reports. COUNTER-VOICE: none critical; the closest is Kipyego's account of failing to take away her kick and the Guardian's bookmakers' scepticism about the marathon. Every effort and preparation claim is largely her own statement, so confidence stays <= 0.62 and no score exceeds 72.
NOT OPENED: the Olympics.com profile (archive blocked), Olympedia and the World Athletics profile page, Letsrun 2016 interview (blocked/empty), Athletics Africa and other race reports, her own interviews on training, Wikipedia. EXCLUDED: marriage and family, injuries and health, her 2013 London withdrawal, nutrition and any doping speculation (no source read raised any), endorsements (Ethiopian Airlines ambassadorship seen only in a search snippet), and the Britannica sentence on her marriage. Five rows; sparse because the sources record results, race tactics and her own statements, not independent accounts of her training.
